name: Clovis culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from fluted stone spear points, campsites and kill sites dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Mobile hunter-gatherers of Ice Age North America, named after finds near Clovis, New Mexico. Their large fluted spear points turn up across much of the continent, often with the bones of mammoths, mastodons and bison. Once thought to be the first Americans, they are now known to have been preceded by earlier people at sites such as Paisley Caves, though some of those pre-Clovis dates are still argued over.

name: Valdivia culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from village sites, pottery and small stone and clay figurines, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: One of the earliest settled, pottery-making cultures of the Americas, on the coast of Ecuador around the Santa Elena peninsula. Valdivia villages such as Real Alto had houses around plazas and ceremonial mounds; people farmed, fished and gathered shellfish. Their pottery is among the oldest in the Americas, and they made many small clay figurines, each with its own hairstyle.

name: Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) civilization
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from about 30 large sites dated by radiocarbon, mostly excavated since the 1990s.
summary: The oldest known civilization in the Americas, in four small river valleys of Peru's north-central coast: the Fortaleza, Pativilca, Supe and Huaura. Its people built large platform mounds and sunken circular plazas at as many as 30 centres, including Caral, without pottery. Irrigation from the snow-fed rivers was key to farming, and coastal towns such as Áspero lived largely from the sea. It declined around 1800 BCE.

name: Poverty Point culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from earthworks, stone tools and imported stone, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Late Archaic hunter-fisher-gatherers of the lower Mississippi Valley who built the great earthworks at Poverty Point in Louisiana. Their settlements stretched more than 100 miles across the Mississippi Delta and south toward the Gulf Coast. They traded for stone over long distances, including soapstone vessels from the Appalachian foothills, and showed that monuments did not need farming.

name: Olmec culture (early)
dateLabel: c. 1400–400 BCE (shown here until c. 650 BCE)
evidenceNote: A few Olmec carvings and the Cascajal Block may carry signs, but nothing can be read, so knowledge comes from excavation.
summary: The earliest major civilization of Mesoamerica, in the hot, wet lowlands of southern Veracruz and western Tabasco, Mexico. Its centres, first San Lorenzo and then La Venta, carved colossal basalt heads, thrones and fine jade. Olmec art and ideas spread widely. This layer draws its heartland before 650 BCE; from then on the map's own 'Olmec Civilization' state polygon takes over.

name: Early Zapotec villages (Valley of Oaxaca)
evidenceNote: Mostly archaeology; a carved stone of about 600 BCE may hold the first Zapotec glyphs, but it can barely be read.
summary: Farming villages of the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico before Monte Albán was founded, led by San José Mogote. Over a thousand years they built palisades, ceremonial platforms, adobe buildings, terraces and small irrigation ditches, and by about 600 BCE carved what may be the first Zapotec writing. Around 500 BCE their people founded Monte Albán; from then the map's own 'Zapotec Civilization' state takes over.

name: Preclassic Maya
dateLabel: c. 1000 BCE – 250 CE (shown here until c. 250 BCE)
evidenceNote: The earliest Maya writing, from about 300 BCE at San Bartolo, can be dated but mostly not yet read; the rest is archaeology.
summary: The early centuries of Maya civilization in the lowlands of Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico and the highlands around Kaminaljuyu. Farming villages grew into cities with huge pyramids, such as El Mirador, joined by causeways, and painted murals and the first Maya hieroglyphs appeared at San Bartolo. This layer draws the Maya area until about 250 BCE, when the map's own 'Mayan City-States' polygon begins.

name: Chavín culture
dateLabel: c. 900–250 BCE (some scholars: from c. 1200 BCE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dated by radiocarbon, but scholars disagree on when it began and when its temple was at its height.
summary: The main culture of Peru's Early Horizon, centred on the temple of Chavín de Huántar in the northern highlands. Its art of fanged gods, jaguars, snakes and birds spread along the coast and highlands, with advances in metalwork and textiles and close ties to the temple's religious cult. Its centre declined after social upheaval around 500–300 BCE.

name: Paracas culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known mostly from cemeteries on the Paracas Peninsula dug since the 1920s, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
summary: An Andean society of the Ica region on Peru's south coast, known for its cemeteries on the Paracas Peninsula. Its people mastered irrigation and made superb embroidered textiles and painted pottery. Communities were run by local chiefs rather than a single ruler. The earliest Nazca Lines were made by Paracas people, and the Nazca culture that followed was strongly influenced by it.

name: Nazca culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from pottery, textiles, the Nazca Lines and sites such as Cahuachi, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
summary: The people of the river valleys of the Rio Grande de Nazca and Ica on Peru's dry south coast, heirs of Paracas. They made brightly painted pottery and textiles, created most of the Nazca Lines, and dug puquios, underground aqueducts, some still working today. Cahuachi was their great pilgrimage centre.

name: Moche culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from huge adobe temples, rich tombs and painted pottery, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: A civilization of Peru's north coast valleys, from the Lambayeque area south to the Moche and beyond. Probably a group of related kingdoms rather than one empire, it built adobe pyramids such as the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, buried lords in rich tombs like Sipán, and is famous for elaborately painted pottery, gold work and irrigation systems.

name: Tiwanaku (early)
dateLabel: c. 100–1050 CE (early phase to c. 500 CE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; its founding date is debated, with careful radiocarbon work pointing to about 110 CE rather than older claims.
summary: A society centred on the city of Tiwanaku near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia. From modest beginnings it grew in power across the Titicaca basin in 200–500 CE and peaked around 500–600 CE and later, building stone platforms and courts and spreading its religious art. This layer draws only its early home area; it later influenced lands far to the south and west.

name: Adena culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from burial mounds and their contents, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Related Early Woodland societies of the Ohio Valley that shared a burial and ceremonial tradition, centred on Ohio and reaching into Kentucky, West Virginia, Indiana and neighbouring states. They built earthen burial mounds, the largest surviving one being Grave Creek Mound, and perhaps the Great Serpent Mound.

name: Hopewell tradition
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from earthworks, mounds and traded objects, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Not one people but a network of Middle Woodland communities in the Eastern Woodlands, linked by trade and shared ceremonies. Its heartlands, in southern Ohio and the Illinois River valley, have huge geometric earthworks and burial mounds with ornaments of copper, mica and obsidian brought from hundreds of miles away. Its exchange network reached from Lake Ontario to Florida.

sources.title: US National Park Service: Hopewell Culture National Historical Park

name: Basketmaker culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from dry caves and pit-house villages, dated by radiocarbon and tree rings.
summary: The ancestors of the Ancestral Puebloans in the Four Corners region of the American Southwest, named for the many fine baskets found in dry caves. They began growing maize while still moving with the seasons; in Late Basketmaker II (about 50–500 CE) they settled in pit-houses, and in Basketmaker III (about 500–750 CE) they took up the bow and arrow and pottery.

name: Green Sahara hunter-fishers and herders
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from campsites, burials, animal bones and rock art, dated by radiocarbon; rock art itself is hard to date.
summary: During the African Humid Period the Sahara had lakes, grassland and wildlife. Hunter-fishers such as the Kiffian people of Gobero lived by lakes, and from about 6000 BCE herders spread cattle, sheep and goats across the region, as the rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer shows. As the rains failed between about 4000 and 3000 BCE, the Sahara dried out and people moved away or adapted.

name: Pastoral Neolithic of eastern Africa
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from animal bones, stone bowls, pottery and burial monuments, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: The first herders of eastern Africa. Around 3000 BCE cattle, sheep and goat herders arrived around Lake Turkana and built monumental cemeteries such as the Lothagam North Pillar Site. Later herders, including the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic peoples with their stone bowls and burial cairns, spread through the Rift Valley of Kenya and northern Tanzania.

sources.title: Hildebrand et al. 2018, PNAS: A monumental cemetery built by eastern Africa's first herders near Lake Turkana, Kenya

name: Kintampo complex
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from village sites, pottery and stone tools, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Early farming and herding villages in central Ghana and neighbouring Côte d'Ivoire and Togo, a step from foraging to settled life in West Africa. Kintampo people lived in villages of wattle-and-daub houses, sometimes on stone foundations, kept cattle, goats and dogs, and made polished stone beads, bracelets and puzzling grooved stone 'rasps'. Pearl millet farming spread to the region at this time.

name: Tichitt tradition
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from hundreds of stone-walled villages, dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Herders and millet farmers of the escarpments of southeastern Mauritania, at Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Walata, Dhar Néma and Dhar Tagant, when the area was savanna. They built some 500 drystone villages with compounds, granaries and tumuli, and are thought to be ancestors of the Soninke people, whose descendants later lived in the region of the Ghana Empire.

name: Nok culture
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from terracotta sculptures, settlements and iron furnaces, dated by radiocarbon and luminescence.
summary: An Iron Age people of central Nigeria, named after the village of Nok where their sculptures were first found in 1928. From about 900 BCE they made hollow terracotta figures and heads with striking eyes and elaborate hairstyles, probably for funeral customs, and by the 4th–3rd centuries BCE some of their sites, such as Taruga, were smelting iron.

name: Bantu expansion (approximate)
evidenceNote: This is a reconstruction from languages, genes and archaeology; its routes and dates are approximate and still debated, so the shapes here are only rough guides.
summary: The spread of Bantu-speaking peoples, with farming, pottery and later iron, from a homeland around the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands across much of central, eastern and southern Africa. Many scholars see a western stream through or along the rainforest reaching central Angola, and an eastern stream reaching west of Lake Victoria by about 500 BCE, then spreading south to reach South Africa by about 300 CE. It happened over many centuries, not as a single migration.

name: Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite (Dʿmt)
dateLabel: c. 800–50 BCE (Dʿmt c. 8th–6th century BCE, dates uncertain)
evidenceNote: A few inscriptions in South Arabian script name the kingdom of Dʿmt and its kings, but they are scarce and their dates uncertain; most knowledge comes from sites such as Yeha.
summary: The highland societies of Eritrea and northern Tigray before the Kingdom of Aksum. A kingdom called Dʿmt, probably with its capital at Yeha, built Sabaean-style temples and wrote in South Arabian script, showing close ties across the Red Sea. Whether Dʿmt became Aksum or was absorbed by it is unknown. This layer stops at about 50 BCE, when the map's own 'Kingdom of Axum' begins.
